cards.explanation: The servants are waiting for their master returning home. Jesus says they're like “…servants waiting for their master to return from the wedding banquet…” (Luke 12:36). It's like leaving the porch light on for someone you love, except these servants are also dressed and ready to go. Nobody's waiting for anyone else in these verses, friends.

The word is "once." The master is coming back from a wedding banquet, and Jesus says the ready servants “…can open the door for him at once.” (Luke 12:36). No digging for keys, no yelling 'one minute!' through the door. Ready servants just open up.

The master waits on them at the table. Jesus says, “…he will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them.” (Luke 12:37). The master is the one doing the serving, friends. I've been serving cookies a long time, and I've never seen that coming either.

The answer is True. Jesus says, “Even if he comes in the second or third watch of the night and finds them alert, those servants will be blessed.” (Luke 12:38). Late hours don't change it, bakers. What counts is that they're alert when he comes.

The answer is False. Jesus says, “If the homeowner had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into.” (Luke 12:39). If he'd known the hour, he could have stopped it. Since he doesn't know, he has to stay ready all along, friends.

The two words are "ready" and "expect." Jesus says, “You also must be ready…” (Luke 12:40). It's the same call He opened with, dressed for service and lamps burning. Then He says the Son of Man “…will come at an hour you do not expect.” (Luke 12:40). So nobody gets to plan around it, friends. That's why He says to be ready.

Peter wants to know whether the parable is for them or for everyone. Peter, one of Jesus's disciples, asks, “Lord, are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” (Luke 12:41). He wants to know who's meant to hear it. That's a good question to ask out loud, friends.

The manager's job is to give the servants their portion on time. Jesus says the master puts the manager in charge of his servants “…to give them their portion at the proper time?” (Luke 12:42). So the job is to get everyone their share when it's due. Faithful and wise means doing that, bakers.

The answer is True. Jesus says, “Blessed is that servant whose master finds him doing so when he returns. Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.” (Luke 12:43-44). Faithful work gets a big reward, friends. That's the master's answer to a job done well.

The servant says his master will be a long time coming. Jesus says the servant says in his heart, “…‘My master will be a long time in coming,’…” (Luke 12:45). It's the 'no rush, he's not here yet' kind of thinking. It's a lot like telling yourself 'I'll just rest my eyes' while the oven timer is running.

The answer is False. Jesus says, “The master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not anticipate.” (Luke 12:46). That servant doesn't see it coming, friends. I think this one is a heavy passage, so take your time with it.

The answer is False. The servant who knows his master's will but doesn't get ready or follow his instructions “…will be beaten with many blows.” (Luke 12:47). The one who unknowingly does things worthy of punishment gets “…few blows.” (Luke 12:48). I think this is a heavy one, friends, but it shows that knowing carries weight.
The word is "much." Jesus says, “From everyone who has been given much, much will be required…” (Luke 12:48). The more someone is given, the more is asked of them, bakers. That one keeps me honest.
